headline: High: shared filesystem and broad write/network defaults make Cline↔Goose prone to prompt injection, data leakage, and conflicting writes.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cline and Goose both expose filesystem and MCP surfaces, and both can read/write workspace files by default. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge if one agent consumes the other's files or MCP outputs as trusted input. The profiles do not prove a direct parser bridge, so medium is the higher justified severity.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other agent's generated files as instructions or prompts, injection becomes actionable.
IF a shared MCP server returns attacker-controlled text that either agent treats as trusted, the pathway is active.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces.
Disable MCP servers that are not strictly required.
Review generated files before the other agent consumes them.
Use a read-only handoff directory for inter-agent exchange.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to all shared artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad filesystem read/write and network egress, so data in a shared workspace can flow into either agent's context and then out to configured model providers or MCP servers. The profiles show source code and files in cwd/workspace as touched data, which makes leakage plausible in default use. No stronger residency or secret-class mismatch is documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace directory, files can be exposed to both contexts.
IF either agent sends workspace contents to its configured model provider or MCP server, those contents can leave the local machine.
mitigations: Use separate repositories or clones per agent.
Remove secrets from the shared workspace immediately.
Restrict network egress for one agent during sensitive tasks.
Store sensitive files outside both agents' readable paths.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on the workspace.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cline and Goose both have execute_shell, install_packages, modify_git_state, write_filesystem, and broad network egress, while both share state via filesystem. In a shared repo, concurrent writes and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state without locking. This matches the high-risk overlap pattern because both agents can mutate the same resources by default.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same git checkout, concurrent commits or file edits can conflict.
IF either agent runs package installs in the shared environment, dependency state can diverge or break the other agent.
mitigations: Assign each agent its own checkout.
Serialize git and package operations manually.
Pause one agent while the other writes.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add file and git locks around shared mutable state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Both agents can act on files and shell commands, so one agent's output can become the other's input without a built-in verification step. Cline's browser and MCP tooling can generate untrusted artifacts, and Goose can consume files and act on them, creating a plausible chain from generated content to downstream action. The profiles do not show fully autonomous external actions, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Goose treats Cline-produced files or browser-derived text as authoritative, errors can cascade into shell or git actions.
IF Cline forwards unverified browser or MCP output into Goose, downstream actions may amplify mistakes.
mitigations: Require human review before handoff.
Pass only minimal structured outputs between agents.
Add a verification checklist for any generated facts.
Keep browser-derived content out of execution paths.
requires-engineering: implement schema validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source coding agents with no documented residency, certification, or retention mismatch. The only concrete compliance-relevant difference is that Cline touches browser screenshots while Goose touches files in cwd, but the profiles do not show a regulated-data violation. Because the rubric requires documented gaps for low, this remains low rather than none.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace, both agents may process it under undocumented retention policies.
IF an operator relies on either agent for residency-bound data handling, the lack of documented controls becomes relevant.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents.
Use synthetic or redacted inputs.
Review vendor retention settings before use.
Avoid mixing jurisdictions in the same workspace.
requires-engineering: obtain and document compliance controls from both vendors.
